question: Whose account of power survives on a palace wall?
summary: At Kalhu, now Nimrud, making a royal palace joined skilled material work, protective imagery and claims about conquest and settlement. A later archive also preserves administrative commands concerning captives. These different sources explain how royal institutions represented power and sought practical results, while keeping the people subjected to those decisions distinct from the official voices that survive.

sections.title: Making a royal centre
sections.text: Ashurnasirpal II made Kalhu, now Nimrud, a royal capital during his reign of 883–859 BCE. His Northwest Palace gathered rooms and courtyards into a setting for royal business, ceremony and residence. Building such a place joined materials and skilled work: mud brick formed its walls, while large slabs of local gypsum lined selected interiors. Quarrying, moving, carving and painting those slabs made authority into a substantial environment that people could enter.

sections.title: Protection around the ruler
sections.text: The surviving panel shows a bird-headed winged figure wearing patterned clothing and holding a bucket. The museum interprets such figures as protective beings. Doorways and rooms made their placement consequential: protection and royal power were presented together as people moved through the building. The throne room also carried scenes of warfare and hunting, while protective imagery appeared widely elsewhere. The palace therefore offered more than a record of events; its makers arranged a particular account of power.

citations.locator: 32.143.7: Description, Artwork Details and inspected local full image
Protective figures, throne-room imagery and doorways

sections.title: The king claims a city
sections.text: Writing ran across many reliefs. In the recurring Standard Inscription, the king named divine supporters, victories and palace materials. He also claimed to have rebuilt Kalhu and settled there people taken from conquered territories. That passage connects the splendid building programme to coercive movement of people. It supplies the ruler’s account of settlement, rather than the voices of those moved. Neither a carved figure nor this text identifies the legal status of every quarry worker, carver or palace servant.

sections.title: Keeping the institution working
sections.text: The palace was also a place of storage, preparation and administration. Excavated rooms and finds help researchers identify these practical activities: Room ZZ contained an oven and cooking vessels, while other areas held stores and archives. These remains come from a building used and altered over generations. Their dates matter. A plan can locate rooms and show relationships between them, but a composite excavated plan cannot make every room or activity contemporary with Ashurnasirpal.

citations.locator: Managing the palace; Behind the scenes, Room ZZ; After Assurnasirpal; Image 1 composite palace plan

sections.title: Another official voice survives
sections.text: A later letter from the palace archive, assigned by its editors to about 732 BCE, orders officials to provision captives and care for sick people among them. It reveals responsibilities and threats inside imperial administration. The order does not prove that its recipients complied. This eighth-century record expands the reference context without changing this case’s ninth-century dates. Reading wall, plan and letter together exposes different institutional purposes; none gives everyone governed by Assyria an equal voice.

deeperReading.title: Read an arrangement, then ask about its date
deeperReading.text: A palace plan lets us ask how activities were placed in relation to one another. The published Northwest Palace drawing locates the throne room B, courtyards and southern service spaces. Robson’s account links Room ZZ with an oven and cooking vessels, and identifies northern areas with administration and storage. These functional readings combine architecture and finds; a room label is not an ancient sign naming its occupants. The drawing also includes later features. It should be read as a composite of excavated remains, with the north arrow and scale retained, rather than a snapshot of one reign. The modern museum arrangement creates another layer: gathering panels from different rooms helps visitors compare them, but changes their architectural relationships. That useful display should be distinguished from evidence of an intact ancient room.

deeperReading.title: An order is evidence of a system, not its successful outcome
deeperReading.text: The later letter names two officials and makes captives their responsibility. Its surviving text combines provision with a threat against neglect. That detail shows how the king sought to make subordinates answerable within a coercive institution. The words do not establish that food reached everyone, that sick people recovered or that those moved consented. Its damaged passages and the editors’ proposed date must travel with any excerpt. Comparing it with the Standard Inscription reveals a useful difference: a public royal claim celebrates achievement, while an administrative command seeks action. Both speak from positions of authority. People subjected to those decisions are present in their content, but their own accounts are absent from these selected sources.

evidenceReading.title: What different official sources can establish
evidenceReading.introduction: These editorial paraphrases distinguish visible detail, royal claims and administrative commands. They are not quotations. The later letter is separate from the selected ninth-century case.

items.label: A visible figure and an interpreted purpose
items.text: The selected photograph visibly preserves a bird head, wings, patterned garments, a bucket and a horizontal band of writing.
items.interpretation: The Met places this figure within protective palace imagery. Its purpose follows from specialist interpretation and architectural context, not from a photograph alone. A learner can support a claim about deliberate visual detail, then identify which further claim requires the museum’s contextual explanation.

items.label: People in the king’s building claim
items.text: The edited Standard Inscription states that the ruler rebuilt Kalhu and settled conquered people there.
items.interpretation: The claim makes forced relocation part of the king’s representation of a successful capital. It does not establish every relocated person’s task or status. The passage prevents a building account from treating resources and labor as if they arrived without political decisions or consequences for people.

citations.locator: Q004477, lines 14b–17a

items.label: Commands and outcomes are different evidence
items.text: SAA 19 006 assigns responsibility for captives and threatens officials against neglect; its reverse also directs care of sick captives.
items.interpretation: This is evidence of intended administration and compulsion, rather than proof that every instruction was fulfilled or that captivity was benign. Ask what a receipt, material distribution record or a captive’s account might add. Do not invent one of those missing sources.

items.label: A plan gathers different dates
items.text: The published plan identifies rooms and courtyards, but also includes later features from the palace’s long history. Its north arrow points near the upper edge and its printed scale runs 0–50 m.
items.interpretation: Room positions and architectural relationships can be discussed without making every drawn feature contemporary. The source plan must retain its date/scale explanation and cannot be treated as a recovered route through one untouched room.

review.reviewer: Codex selected-source consultation and internal author QA; not independent historian approval
review.scope: Bounded main/deeper account, paired royal and administrative source interpretation, inspected local figure and composite source plan, concrete supplied-image inquiry and separate phased reference context. Full original case interval, original objects, coordinates, dimensions and existing claims preserved.
limitations: Selected project webpages and two online primary editions, not whole excavation books, every inscription exemplar, full SAA 19 volume or a complete archive. Q004477 is a composite scholarly edition, not a fresh transcription from Met 32.143.7.

The captives letter is undated with proposed c.732 BCE placement, later than the selected reign. Orders, threats, consent and successful outcomes remain distinct; broken/restored passages are not treated as complete secure text. No universal slave status for all palace workers inferred.

The small 460×926 palace plan is composite and includes later features. It is not a single 883–859 phase survey; internal room coordinates, exact visitor itineraries and newly recovered image detail are not supplied. The unmodified drawing carries CC BY-SA 3.0 attribution and a readable room/phase text equivalent; its original small labels remain small.

Earlier direct Met catalogue access returned 429/tool failures; subsequent consultation renewed the official Description, Artwork Details and Public Domain statement. Source-access failures remain in dated research notes rather than being presented as successful earlier consultation.

placeStudy.title: Different Assyrian royal centres in time
placeStudy.description: Three city references orient the Met account of changing royal capitals. Their roles belong to different reigns. The separate composite palace plan supplies architectural detail at Kalhu; this regional panel does not reconstruct that plan, a military route, an ancient river bankline or imperial borders.
